claim: Most yeast cells arrest in G1 before death.
source: We show that most yeast cells arrest in G1 before death with low nuclear levels of Cln3, a key G1 cyclin extremely sensitive to chaperone status.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D showing that ca. 75% of cells die in the T1 period of G1.

claim: Aging yeast cells display low nuclear levels of Cln3 before death.
source: We show that most yeast cells arrest in G1 before death with low nuclear levels of Cln3, a key G1 cyclin extremely sensitive to chaperone status.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-H demonstrating decreased nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio of mCtr-Cln311A after the last budding event.

claim: Cln3 is a key G1 cyclin extremely sensitive to chaperone status.
source: We show that most yeast cells arrest in G1 before death with low nuclear levels of Cln3, a key G1 cyclin extremely sensitive to chaperone status.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Moreno et al., 2019; Parisi et al., 2018; Vergés et al., 2007) showing chaperone dependence of Cln3.

claim: Chaperone availability is seriously compromised in aged cells.
source: Chaperone availability is seriously compromised in aged cells, and the G1 arrest coincides with massive aggregation of a metastable chaperone-activity reporter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2B-C showing dramatic drops in mobility of Ssa1 and Ydj1 chaperones in aged cells measured by FLIP and RICS.

claim: The G1 arrest in aging cells coincides with massive aggregation of a metastable chaperone-activity reporter.
source: Chaperone availability is seriously compromised in aged cells, and the G1 arrest coincides with massive aggregation of a metastable chaperone-activity reporter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D-E showing FFL-GFP aggregation beginning around the last budding event and increasing until death.

claim: G1-cyclin overexpression increases lifespan in a chaperone-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, G1-cyclin overexpression increases lifespan in a chaperone-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C showing increased lifespan with CLN3 overexpression, and Figure 5F showing that the effect requires Ydj1.

claim: Enforced protein aggregation causes a severe reduction in lifespan.
source: As a key prediction of a model integrating autocatalytic protein aggregation and a minimal Start network, enforced protein aggregation causes a severe reduction in lifespan, an effect that is greatly alleviated by increased expression of specific chaperones or cyclin Cln3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A showing that PFD expression dramatically decreases lifespan.

claim: The lifespan reduction caused by enforced protein aggregation is greatly alleviated by increased expression of specific chaperones.
source: As a key prediction of a model integrating autocatalytic protein aggregation and a minimal Start network, enforced protein aggregation causes a severe reduction in lifespan, an effect that is greatly alleviated by increased expression of specific chaperones or cyclin Cln3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7F-G showing partial suppression of PFD-induced lifespan reduction by chaperone overexpression.

claim: The lifespan reduction caused by enforced protein aggregation is greatly alleviated by increased expression of cyclin Cln3.
source: As a key prediction of a model integrating autocatalytic protein aggregation and a minimal Start network, enforced protein aggregation causes a severe reduction in lifespan, an effect that is greatly alleviated by increased expression of specific chaperones or cyclin Cln3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7H showing complete suppression of PFD-induced lifespan reduction by CLN3 overexpression.

claim: Proteostasis breakdown compromises chaperone activity and G1-cyclin function, causing an irreversible arrest in G1.
source: Overall, our data show that proteostasis breakdown, by compromising chaperone activity and G1-cyclin function, causes an irreversible arrest in G1, configuring a molecular pathway postulating proteostasis decay as a key contributing effector of cell senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by the integration of multiple experimental observations including chaperone mobility defects (Figure 2), Cln3 nuclear exclusion (Figure 1), and protein aggregation timing (Figure 3).

claim: Yeast daughter cells are rejuvenated during most of the mother cell lifespan.
source: Since yeast daughter cells are rejuvenated during most of the mother cell lifespan, it is generally accepted that aging is the result of asymmetric segregation of factors such as extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs), dysfunctional mitochondrial and vacuolar compartments, or resilient protein aggregates (Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on yeast aging mechanisms.

claim: Aging is the result of asymmetric segregation of factors such as extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs), dysfunctional mitochondrial and vacuolar compartments, or resilient protein aggregates.
source: Since yeast daughter cells are rejuvenated during most of the mother cell lifespan, it is generally accepted that aging is the result of asymmetric segregation of factors such as extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs), dysfunctional mitochondrial and vacuolar compartments, or resilient protein aggregates (Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review literature on yeast aging.

claim: Proteostasis deterioration is a universal hallmark of cellular aging.
source: Proteostasis deterioration is a universal hallmark of cellular aging (Kaushik and Cuervo, 2015; Klaips et al., 2018; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; López-Otín et al., 2013), and yeast cells have been the paradigm to study the mechanisms of asymmetric segregation of protein aggregates or deposits and their relevance in aging (Hill et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature on aging hallmarks.

claim: Yeast cells have been the paradigm to study the mechanisms of asymmetric segregation of protein aggregates or deposits and their relevance in aging.
source: Proteostasis deterioration is a universal hallmark of cellular aging (Kaushik and Cuervo, 2015; Klaips et al., 2018; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; López-Otín et al., 2013), and yeast cells have been the paradigm to study the mechanisms of asymmetric segregation of protein aggregates or deposits and their relevance in aging (Hill et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review on protein aggregation in yeast aging.

claim: Molecular chaperones play key roles in proteostasis by folding nascent polypeptides, refolding misfolded proteins, and facilitating their degradation or accumulation in different types of aggregates and deposits if they cannot be properly recycled.
source: Molecular chaperones play key roles in proteostasis by folding nascent polypeptides, refolding misfolded proteins, and facilitating their degradation or accumulation in different types of aggregates and deposits if they cannot be properly recycled (Hartl et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on chaperone function.

claim: Yeast cells display an age-dependent protein deposit, termed APOD.
source: Yeast cells display an age-dependent protein deposit, termed APOD (Saarikangas and Barral, 2016), that appears early in their replicative lifespan and is retained in the mother cell compartment in every division cycle (Hill et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature describing the APOD.

claim: The APOD appears early in the replicative lifespan and is retained in the mother cell compartment in every division cycle.
source: Yeast cells display an age-dependent protein deposit, termed APOD (Saarikangas and Barral, 2016), that appears early in their replicative lifespan and is retained in the mother cell compartment in every division cycle (Hill et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on APOD dynamics.

claim: Several chaperones including Hsp104, Ssa1 and Ydj1 co-localize with the APOD.
source: Several chaperones including Hsp104, Ssa1 and Ydj1 co-localize with the APOD (Andersson et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2014; Saarikangas and Barral, 2015), where they are thought to play a concerted role in disaggregation and recycling of deposited proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature showing chaperone localization to the APOD.

claim: Chaperones at the APOD are thought to play a concerted role in disaggregation and recycling of deposited proteins.
source: Several chaperones including Hsp104, Ssa1 and Ydj1 co-localize with the APOD (Andersson et al., 2013; Hill et al., 2014; Saarikangas and Barral, 2015), where they are thought to play a concerted role in disaggregation and recycling of deposited proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the localization data cited and established knowledge of chaperone function.

claim: Farnesylated Ydj1 is important for proper retention of the APOD at the ER in the mother cell compartment.
source: Regarding asymmetric segregation of protein aggregates during cell aging, farnesylated Ydj1 has been shown to be important for proper retention of the APOD at the ER in the mother cell compartment (Saarikangas et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on Ydj1 function in APOD retention.

claim: Hsp104 and Ydj1 are required for a normal replicative lifespan.
source: The functional relevance of chaperones at the crossroads of protein aggregation and replicative aging is supported by the fact that Hsp104 and Ydj1 are required for a normal replicative lifespan and, when overexpressed, Hsp104 restores proteasome activity in aging cells (Andersson et al., 2013) and suppresses lifespan defects of sir2 mutants (Erjavec et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature showing lifespan defects in chaperone mutants.

claim: When overexpressed, Hsp104 restores proteasome activity in aging cells.
source: The functional relevance of chaperones at the crossroads of protein aggregation and replicative aging is supported by the fact that Hsp104 and Ydj1 are required for a normal replicative lifespan and, when overexpressed, Hsp104 restores proteasome activity in aging cells (Andersson et al., 2013) and suppresses lifespan defects of sir2 mutants (Erjavec et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on Hsp104 overexpression effects.

claim: Hsp104 overexpression suppresses lifespan defects of sir2 mutants.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on Hsp104 suppression of sir2 mutant phenotypes.

claim: Overexpression of metacaspase Mca1 extends the lifespan of yeast mother cells in a Hsp104- and Ydj1-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, by counteracting protein aggregation, overexpression of metacaspase Mca1 extends the lifespan of yeast mother cells in a Hsp104- and Ydj1-dependent manner (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on Mca1 overexpression effects on lifespan.

claim: The interdivision time of yeast cells increases during the last cycles before death.
source: The interdivision time of yeast cells increases during the last cycles before death (Fehrmann et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2012; Lindstrom and Gottschling, 2009) and most aging cells accumulate in the unbudded period before death (Delaney et al., 2013; McVey et al., 2001), suggesting that aging-related processes interfere with the mechanisms that trigger Start to drive cells into the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on cell cycle timing in aging cells.

claim: Most aging cells accumulate in the unbudded period before death.
source: The interdivision time of yeast cells increases during the last cycles before death (Fehrmann et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2012; Lindstrom and Gottschling, 2009) and most aging cells accumulate in the unbudded period before death (Delaney et al., 2013; McVey et al., 2001), suggesting that aging-related processes interfere with the mechanisms that trigger Start to drive cells into the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on cell cycle phase distribution in aging cells.

claim: Aging-related processes interfere with the mechanisms that trigger Start to drive cells into the cell cycle.
source: The interdivision time of yeast cells increases during the last cycles before death (Fehrmann et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2012; Lindstrom and Gottschling, 2009) and most aging cells accumulate in the unbudded period before death (Delaney et al., 2013; McVey et al., 2001), suggesting that aging-related processes interfere with the mechanisms that trigger Start to drive cells into the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the cited observations of G1 accumulation and interdivision time increases.

claim: Cln3 cyclin is a rate-limiting activator of Start that is maintained at low but nearly constant levels during G1.
source: The Cln3 cyclin is a rate-limiting activator of Start that is maintained at low but nearly constant levels during G1 (Tyers et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on Cln3 function and regulation.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of Cln3 is driven by a constitutive C-terminal nuclear-localization signal (NLS).
source: Nuclear accumulation of Cln3 is driven by a constitutive C-terminal nuclear-localization signal (NLS) (Edgington and Futcher, 2001; Miller and Cross, 2001), but involves the essential participation of Ssa1 (or paralog Ssa2) and Ydj1 chaperones (Vergés et al., 2007) and the segregase activity of Cdc48 to release the G1 cyclin from the ER (Parisi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on Cln3 nuclear localization mechanisms.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of Cln3 involves the essential participation of Ssa1 (or paralog Ssa2) and Ydj1 chaperones.
source: Nuclear accumulation of Cln3 is driven by a constitutive C-terminal nuclear-localization signal (NLS) (Edgington and Futcher, 2001; Miller and Cross, 2001), but involves the essential participation of Ssa1 (or paralog Ssa2) and Ydj1 chaperones (Vergés et al., 2007) and the segregase activity of Cdc48 to release the G1 cyclin from the ER (Parisi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on chaperone requirements for Cln3 function.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of Cln3 involves the segregase activity of Cdc48 to release the G1 cyclin from the ER.
source: Nuclear accumulation of Cln3 is driven by a constitutive C-terminal nuclear-localization signal (NLS) (Edgington and Futcher, 2001; Miller and Cross, 2001), but involves the essential participation of Ssa1 (or paralog Ssa2) and Ydj1 chaperones (Vergés et al., 2007) and the segregase activity of Cdc48 to release the G1 cyclin from the ER (Parisi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on Cdc48 function in Cln3 localization.

claim: Ssa1 and Ydj1 affect Cln3 stability.
source: In addition, Ssa1 and Ydj1 also affect Cln3 stability (Truman et al., 2012; Yaglom et al., 1996), and their availability modulates the execution of Start as a function of growth and stress (Moreno et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on chaperone effects on Cln3 stability.

claim: Chaperone availability modulates the execution of Start as a function of growth and stress.

claim: The average interdivision time was rather constant during aging until the senescence-entry point (SEP).
source: As previously observed, the average interdivision time was rather constant during aging until the senescence-entry point (SEP) (Fehrmann et al., 2013), when it displayed an abrupt increase that was maintained for ca. 2–3 generations on average prior to cell death (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At the SEP, interdivision time displays an abrupt increase that is maintained for ca. 2–3 generations on average prior to cell death.
source: As previously observed, the average interdivision time was rather constant during aging until the senescence-entry point (SEP) (Fehrmann et al., 2013), when it displayed an abrupt increase that was maintained for ca. 2–3 generations on average prior to cell death (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The SEP concurs with an increase in the length of both unbudded (G1) and budded (S-G2-M) phases of the cycle.
source: The SEP concurred with an increase in the length of both unbudded (G1) and budded (S-G2-M) phases of the cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

source: Finally, old cells selected with the mother-enrichment program (MEP) displayed a larger fraction in G1 compared to young mother cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).

source: Execution of Start is particularly sensitive to growth, and cells arrest in G1 when deprived of essential nutrients.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and is an inference from the combination of constant growth rate and extended G1.

source: Although the differences were not as large as previously reported (Neurohr et al., 2018), Whi5 levels in the nucleus displayed a 3-fold increase during the last cycles and the final arrest in G1.

source: Cln3 is the most upstream G1 cyclin acting in the positive feedback loop that inactivates Whi5 and executes Start (Skotheim et al., 2008; Tyers et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on Start regulation.

claim: Cln3 is too short-lived to be detected as a fluorescent-protein fusion in single cells.
source: Since Cln3 is too short-lived to be detected as a fluorescent-protein fusion in single cells, we used a hyperstable and hypoactive Cln311A protein fused to mCitrine (mCtr-Cln311A) that can be detected by fluorescence microscopy with no gross effects on cell cycle progression (Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Cln3 stability and citation to literature describing the stabilized variant.

claim: mCtr-Cln311A can be detected by fluorescence microscopy with no gross effects on cell cycle progression.
source: Since Cln3 is too short-lived to be detected as a fluorescent-protein fusion in single cells, we used a hyperstable and hypoactive Cln311A protein fused to mCitrine (mCtr-Cln311A) that can be detected by fluorescence microscopy with no gross effects on cell cycle progression (Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature characterizing the mCtr-Cln311A reporter.

claim: mCtr-Cln311A displays a distinct nuclear signal during the last cycles before the final budding event.
source: As expected from its essential role in the nucleus, mCtr-Cln311A displayed a distinct nuclear signal during the last cycles before the final budding event (Figure 1G,H, and Video 2); however, the nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio decreased to very low levels afterwards and remained low until death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H and Video 2.

claim: After the final budding event, the nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio of mCtr-Cln311A decreases to very low levels and remains low until death.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H and Video 2.

claim: CLN3 mRNA levels do not show significant changes in aged cells.
source: In agreement with the fact that CLN3 mRNA levels do not show significant changes in aged cells (Janssens et al., 2015; Yiu et al., 2008), overall cellular levels of mCtr-Cln311A remained rather constant and similar to young cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), ruling out major effects due to transcriptional or translational regulation of Cln3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies of aging cells.

claim: Overall cellular levels of mCtr-Cln311A remain rather constant and similar to young cells.
source: In agreement with the fact that CLN3 mRNA levels do not show significant changes in aged cells (Janssens et al., 2015; Yiu et al., 2008), overall cellular levels of mCtr-Cln311A remained rather constant and similar to young cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), ruling out major effects due to transcriptional or translational regulation of Cln3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Major effects due to transcriptional or translational regulation of Cln3 in aging are ruled out.

evidence: This claim is an inference based on the constant mRNA and protein levels observed.

claim: Aging cells undergo profound alterations in the mechanisms that drive nuclear accumulation of cyclin Cln3.
source: In summary, our data suggest that aging cells would undergo profound alterations in the mechanisms that drive nuclear accumulation of cyclin Cln3 and, hence, delay G1 progression as observed in the last cycles before cell death.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed decrease in nuclear Cln3 despite constant total levels.

claim: Alterations in Cln3 nuclear accumulation mechanisms delay G1 progression in the last cycles before cell death.
source: In summary, our data suggest that aging cells would undergo profound alterations in the mechanisms that drive nuclear accumulation of cyclin Cln3 and, hence, delay G1 progression as observed in the last cycles before cell death.

claim: Observed changes in chaperone concentrations agree with previous analysis at the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Observed changes in chaperone concentrations agree with previous analysis at the mRNA (Yiu et al., 2008) and protein (Janssens et al., 2015) levels, and suggest that cells sense proteostasis defects and, regarding to Hsp104, react during aging similarly to other stress instances in which chaperone availability is assumed to be temporarily compromised (de Nadal et al., 2011).

claim: Cells sense proteostasis defects and react during aging similarly to other stress instances in which chaperone availability is assumed to be temporarily compromised.
